title: Species of larger genera more often present varieties

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species of larger genera more often present varieties

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it has invariably proved to be the case that a larger proportion of the species on the side of the larger genera present varieties, than on the side of the smaller genera.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera”. Scope: plants of regional floras and beetles of local faunas

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-08: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.87

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variables are directly represented in global public taxonomic databases and analysis is simple. Replication across regions and clades can expose taxonomic-practice confounding.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within regions and major clades, regress the proportion of species with accepted varieties and varieties per varying species on genus species richness, controlling sampling effort. A consistent positive relationship supports the claim; zero or negative effects refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Variety rank is used unevenly among clades.

Taxonomic effort is greater in species-rich genera.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.81
analysis feasibility: 0.86
operationalizability: 0.92
discriminating power: 0.83
data existence: 0.92

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison is a direct contingency table of genus size against variety counts, and floras plus name catalogues supply it for many countries' plants. Infraspecific ranks are incomplete and effort-biased, so discriminating power sits at the level of a correctable confound rather than a clean test. Animal groups in the original scope would need extra compilation beyond the plant floras.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within each country or regional biota, compare the proportion of species that have named varieties, and the mean number of varieties, between species in genera above and below the median genus size. Higher proportions and means on the large-genus side, after controlling for study effort, would support the pattern; a null or reversed difference would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Beetle faunas, part of the original scope, are less consistently digitized than vascular-plant floras.

Large genera are studied more intensively, so they accumulate more named varieties.

Variety rank is used inconsistently and is often omitted from global checklists.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.48
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data existence: 0.64
data adequacy: 0.48
